tips.title: Pythagoras twice, or square all three
tips.body: The space diagonal is either **two 2D Pythagoras steps** — base diagonal first, then with the height — or the one-step $d^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2$. If you ever doubt the formula, do it in two steps: you cannot misremember Pythagoras applied twice.

tips.title: Never round the middle value
tips.body: Carry the **square** of the base diagonal into step 2 rather than a rounded length. Rounding a number you are about to square pushes the error into the final answer, and in a *will it fit* question it can reverse the conclusion.

tips.title: Draw the triangle flat, on its own
tips.body: The hard part of a 3D question is **seeing** the triangle, not solving it. Sketch it away from the box, label all three sides, and it becomes an ordinary 2D problem you have done a hundred times.

tips.title: Will it fit means the space diagonal
tips.body: The longest straight object a box takes is exactly its **space diagonal** — not the longest edge, and not the largest face diagonal. Say that sentence, compare the two numbers explicitly, and state the conclusion: all three are marked.

why.matters:
Pythagoras in three dimensions is the same theorem used twice, and the reason to be comfortable with it is that **the longest straight line in a box is not any of its edges**.

It runs corner to opposite corner, through the middle, and it is longer than anything you can measure along the outside. Anyone who has to fit a long thing into a box — a courier, a carpenter, someone moving house — is asking about that diagonal, whether or not they know its name.

examples.title: Will the pole fit in the box?
examples.body:
A box measures 1.2 m by 0.6 m by 0.4 m. You have a pole 1.35 m long. It is longer than every edge of the box, and longer than the diagonal across the base ($\sqrt{1.2^2 + 0.6^2} = 1.34$ m), so it will not lie flat — does it go in at all?

Take it in two steps. Across the base, the diagonal is $\sqrt{1.2^2 + 0.6^2}$. Then stand that diagonal up as one side of a new right-angled triangle, with the height 0.4 as the other, and the hypotenuse is the line from one bottom corner to the opposite top corner.

In one line that is $\sqrt{1.2^2 + 0.6^2 + 0.4^2} = \sqrt{1.96} = 1.4$ m. So the 1.3 m pole fits, diagonally, with room to spare — even though every single edge of the box is shorter than it.

That is the whole content of the topic, and the reason the formula has three squares under the root rather than two.

visual.alt: A cuboid drawn in oblique projection with the diagonal across its base and the space diagonal from one bottom corner to the opposite top corner both marked

steps.title: From a flat triangle to a box
steps.body:
This topic is **Higher tier**. The Foundation version of this specification point stops at right-angled triangles in **two-dimensional** figures; working in three dimensions is the Higher addition.

In two dimensions, Pythagoras says $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ for a right-angled triangle.

In a **cuboid**, the longest line you can draw is the **space diagonal**, running from one corner to the opposite corner through the middle of the box. Its length comes from the same theorem used **twice**.

1. First find the **diagonal of the base**, using the width and the depth.
2. Then use that diagonal together with the **height**, in a second right-angled triangle standing upright inside the box.

That second triangle is the one students cannot see at first. Its base is the diagonal you just found, lying flat; its height is the vertical edge; and its hypotenuse is the space diagonal.

Doing it in two steps is worth the effort, because it makes the working visible and each step is an ordinary 2D Pythagoras that you already know.

steps.title: The one-step formula
steps.body:
Because the two steps square and add each time, they collapse into a single formula. For a cuboid with edges $a$, $b$ and $c$:

$$d^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2$$

So for our cuboid: $4^2 + 3^2 + 12^2 = 16 + 9 + 144 = 169$, and $\sqrt{169} = 13$ cm. The same answer, in one line.

It is worth knowing **both** routes.

- The **formula** is faster, and it is the one to use under time pressure.
- The **two-step method** is what a question means when it says *show your working*, and it is the only route when the question asks for the **base diagonal** as well, or for an **angle**, which needs that middle triangle anyway.

The formula is also easy to misremember as $a + b + c$ or as $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} + c$. If you are unsure in the exam, do it in two steps: you cannot misremember Pythagoras applied twice.

steps.title: Seeing the right triangle
steps.body:
The real difficulty in 3D questions is **finding the triangle**, not doing the arithmetic. Three habits make it much easier.

**1. Draw the triangle separately.** Sketch it flat, away from the box, with its three sides labelled. Once it is on the page as an ordinary 2D triangle, it is an ordinary 2D problem.

**2. Identify the right angle first.** In a cuboid, a vertical edge meets the base at a right angle. That is what makes the upright triangle right-angled, and it is the fact the whole method depends on.

**3. Work out which lengths you actually have.** The upright triangle's base is usually a **diagonal**, not an edge, so you nearly always have to find it first. Students who go wrong here have used an edge where a diagonal belonged.

A useful check at the end: the space diagonal must be **longer than every edge** and **longer than every face diagonal**. If it is not, something has gone wrong.

steps.title: Going deeper: the pencil-in-a-box question
steps.body:
The application that appears most often is whether an object fits inside a box. The reasoning is short but has to be stated properly.

> A box measures 8 cm by 6 cm by 10 cm. Will a 14 cm pencil fit inside?

**The key idea**: the longest straight object that fits is exactly the **space diagonal**, because that is the longest straight line the box contains.

$$d^2 = 8^2 + 6^2 + 10^2 = 64 + 36 + 100 = 200$$
$$d = \sqrt{200} \approx 14.1 \text{ cm}$$

Since $14.1 > 14$, the pencil **does** fit, though only just.

**Three things a full answer must do.**

1. Say **why** the space diagonal is the relevant length. "The longest line inside a box is its space diagonal" is a marked statement.
2. **Compare** the two numbers explicitly, and state the conclusion. A calculation with no conclusion loses the last mark.
3. Keep enough **accuracy** to make the comparison honest. Rounding $\sqrt{200}$ to 14 makes the answer look borderline when it is not; here the margin is only 0.1 cm, so 1 decimal place is the minimum.

That last point is worth dwelling on. When two numbers are close, the rounding decides the answer, and a question is often designed so that careless rounding gives the wrong conclusion. Work to more figures than you think you need, and round only at the very end.

**A related trap.** The diagonal of the **largest face** is not the longest line in the box. Here the largest face is 8 by 10, with a diagonal of $\sqrt{164} \approx 12.8$ cm — shorter than the space diagonal, and using it would wrongly conclude the pencil does not fit.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- This topic is **Higher tier**; the Foundation specification stops at two-dimensional figures.
- The **space diagonal** is the longest straight line inside a cuboid.
- **Two-step method**: find the **base diagonal** from the width and depth, then use it with the **height**.
- **One-step formula**: $d^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2$.
- For a 4 by 3 by 12 cuboid: base diagonal $5$ cm, space diagonal $13$ cm.
- Use the formula for **speed**; use the two steps when asked to **show working**, or when the base diagonal or an angle is also needed.
- **Never round the middle value.** Carry the unrounded base diagonal into step 2.
- Working backwards: $c^2 = d^2 - a^2 - b^2$, taking the positive root.
- **Draw the triangle flat and separately.** A 3D problem becomes a 2D one as soon as the triangle is on the page.
- The **check**: the space diagonal must be longer than every edge and every face diagonal.
- For *will it fit*, say that the space diagonal is the **longest line the box contains**, compare explicitly, and **state the conclusion**.

questions.prompt: A cuboid measures 6 cm by 6 cm by 3 cm. Find the diagonal of its base and its space diagonal, showing your method, and check your answer using the single formula.
questions.solution: The base of the cuboid is a square measuring six centimetres by six centimetres. Applying Pythagoras to the base gives six squared plus six squared, which is thirty six plus thirty six, or seventy two, so the base diagonal is the square root of seventy two, which is about eight point four nine centimetres. For the second step, imagine a right angled triangle standing upright inside the cuboid, with the base diagonal as its base and the vertical edge of three centimetres as its height. Applying Pythagoras again gives seventy two plus nine, which is eighty one, and the square root of eighty one is exactly nine, so the space diagonal is nine centimetres. Note that the base diagonal was not rounded before being used in the second step; its square, seventy two, was carried forward exactly. Checking with the single formula, six squared plus six squared plus three squared is thirty six plus thirty six plus nine, which is eighty one, and the square root of eighty one is nine, confirming the answer.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Step 1: the base.** It is a 6 by 6 square.

$$6^2 + 6^2 = 36 + 36 = 72$$

Base diagonal $= \sqrt{72} \approx 8.49$ cm.

**Step 2: the upright triangle.** Its base is that diagonal and its height is the 3 cm edge.

$$72 + 3^2 = 72 + 9 = 81$$

Space diagonal $= \sqrt{81} = \mathbf{9}$ cm.

Notice the base diagonal was **not rounded**: its square, 72, went straight into step 2.

**Check with the formula.** $6^2 + 6^2 + 3^2 = 81$, and $\sqrt{81} = 9$ ✓

questions.prompt: A closed box measures 8 cm by 6 cm by 10 cm. A pencil is 14 cm long. Determine whether the pencil will fit inside the box, justifying your answer fully.
questions.solution: The longest straight line that can fit inside a cuboid is its space diagonal, running from one corner to the opposite corner through the middle of the box, so that is the length the pencil must be compared with. Using the formula, the space diagonal squared is eight squared plus six squared plus ten squared, which is sixty four plus thirty six plus one hundred, giving two hundred. The square root of two hundred is fourteen point one four centimetres to two decimal places. Since fourteen point one four centimetres is greater than the fourteen centimetre length of the pencil, the pencil will fit inside the box, although only just, with a margin of about one millimetre. It is worth keeping two decimal places here, because rounding the diagonal to fourteen centimetres would have made the fit look exact rather than clear.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Why the space diagonal.** It is the **longest straight line the box contains**, so a straight pencil fits if and only if it is no longer than that. Saying this is a mark.

**The calculation.**

$$d^2 = 8^2 + 6^2 + 10^2 = 64 + 36 + 100 = 200$$

$$d = \sqrt{200} = 14.14 \text{ cm (2 d.p.)}$$

**The conclusion.** $14.14 > 14$, so the pencil **does fit** — by about a millimetre.

**On accuracy.** Rounding $\sqrt{200}$ to 14 would make a clear fit look exact. With a margin this small, keep the decimals until the comparison is made.

Using the largest **face** diagonal instead, $\sqrt{164} \approx 12.8$ cm, would have given the wrong answer.

examTechnique.body:
Sketch the cuboid, then sketch the triangle you need **separately and flat**. Label every side you know before calculating anything.

Decide which route the question wants. If it says *show your working*, or asks for the base diagonal or an angle as well, use the two-step method. Otherwise the formula is faster.

Carry unrounded values between steps. Squaring a rounded number is how accuracy is lost.

Check the answer against the edges: the space diagonal must be the longest line in the box.

For a *will it fit* question, state that the space diagonal is the longest straight line the box contains, calculate it to enough figures, compare explicitly, and write the conclusion as a sentence.

Give lengths with units, and round only at the end.
examinerErrors: Using an edge where the base diagonal belonged in the second step.
Rounding the base diagonal before squaring it again.
Writing d = a + b + c instead of squaring.
Using the diagonal of the largest face for a 'will it fit' question.
Calculating the diagonal but never comparing it with the object's length.
Giving no conclusion after a correct calculation.
Rounding to a whole number when the margin is a fraction of a centimetre.
Forgetting the units on a length.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer sketches the triangle separately before touching a calculator, which is what turns a three-dimensional problem into one it can already do. It carries exact values between steps and rounds only once, at the end. In a fitting question it states why the space diagonal is the relevant length rather than assuming the reader knows, keeps enough decimal places for the comparison to be honest, and finishes with an explicit conclusion. And it checks the result against the edges, knowing that the space diagonal has to beat every one of them.
